blocks.text: Why do financial advisors push annuities

The push for annuities often stems from the structure of the financial services industry. Advisors are compensated for providing long-term advice and asset management. Annuities provide a stable, predictable income stream for the client, which in turn creates a reliable revenue base for the advisor. This alignment of incentives is often why you see these products prioritized in client portfolios. However, explaining the product structure is where the friction begins. Analysts must translate these complex, multi-year contracts into clear, understandable metrics that show value to the client and the firm.
The problem with explaining product structure

The core issue is a dimensional mismatch. Most companies report financial performance based on legal organizational structures. This does not align with how products actually function or generate value. When you try to map product costs into this rigid framework, you end up with "spaghetti code" models. These are fragile, hard to audit, and nearly impossible to explain to a product manager who just wants to know if their line is profitable.
Why this happens in your models

You are likely dealing with legacy data structures. If your firm reports by cost center, but your analysis needs to be by product line, you are forced to create complex manual workarounds. These workarounds are prone to error. A single change in a product launch date or a shift in operational overhead can break your entire model. This is why stakeholders often distrust the numbers. They see the output, but they cannot follow the logic that got you there.
Fixing the model without buying new software

items: Adopt the 80/20 rule: Focus on the few allocation drivers that account for the bulk of costs. Do not chase 100% precision.
Document your logic: Use a dedicated tab in Excel to explain the formulas and assumptions behind your allocations.
Standardize your inputs: Ensure that all product managers agree on the cost drivers before you start building the model.
Build modular models: Separate data, calculation, and reporting tabs to make your work easier to audit and update.

blocks.text: How Lazur helps you analyze faster

Lazur lives in your Mac notch and acts as a sounding board for your financial models. When you are stuck on a complex formula, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to explain what a specific section of your model is doing. A week plan for better financial modeling

items: Monday: Audit your current model. Identify one area where the logic is opaque and needs documentation.
Tuesday: Simplify your allocation drivers. Remove any that account for less than 5% of total cost.
Wednesday: Create a 'Logic' tab in your model. Use Lazur to dictate the explanation of your key formulas.
Thursday: Review the model with a stakeholder. Ask them to point out where they feel lost.
Friday: Refine the model based on the feedback. Update your documentation to address the confusion points.

faq.question: Why are annuities so hard to model in Excel?
faq.answer: Annuities involve long-term, multi-year cash flow projections with complex surrender charges and variable interest rates. Mapping these into a static spreadsheet often creates fragile dependencies.

faq.question: Should I move away from Excel for complex product modeling?
faq.answer: Excel is the industry standard, but once you exceed three simultaneous editors or require complex audit trails, consider dedicated platforms like Cube or Anaplan.

faq.question: How can I make my financial models more transparent?
faq.answer: Focus on the 80/20 rule for cost allocations, document your assumptions in a dedicated tab, and ensure your model structure is modular.

fixes.title: Apply the 80/20 rule
fixes.text: Identify the top 20% of allocation drivers that account for 80% of costs and focus your analysis there.

fixes.title: Document your logic
